doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: The element of surprise and Joe Williams
summary: Predictable head-solos-fours format puts audiences to sleep; composition and surprise, recalled with Matt Wilson and Joe Williams.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: If there’s something that makes a person, a listener, turn his head and go oh, what was that.

Right. Exactly. And the element of surprise. Matt Wilson had a wonderful workshop yesterday and I advocated also, we have such history now of playing music that is jazz, and we play the head. And then we take solos. And then we take fours. And then the drums do this. So now everybody does it that way. And then we wonder how come audiences are going to sleep. Because it’s all predictable. So the element of surprise — it doesn’t have to be a huge surprise, it just has to be something that’s not predictable. So that’s where the composition has really hit me. Because now you have to write something that somebody else who is coming out of this vein may take the composition this way. And that’s what everybody expects. And all of a sudden you go — and all of a sudden people go like this — and all of a sudden you’ve got their attention. That’s what we can do as players, as improvisers, to do something that people — they’re ready for you and all of a sudden you say, “Oh, that was nice, what did they do?” But all of a sudden they did something. This is where these characters are. It was fun watching Joe Williams because when he was doing “A Child is Born” and when he said “child” his eyes got bit. I said whoa! And it was a beautiful sound coming out. You’ve got to have that element of surprise, to not be so one hundred percent predictable. And a lot of people don’t want that.
